title: Cross products, orientation, and area
objective: Compute ordered three-dimensional cross products, verify perpendicularity, and use their direction and magnitude for area and a supplied torque model.
why: An ordered pair of directions determines an oriented normal. The cross product packages that direction with an area magnitude, which makes it useful for geometry and supplied torque models. Its order and result type differ from the dot product.

sections.heading: Quick recall
paragraphs: In a right-handed orthonormal three-dimensional frame, $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\ u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\ u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$. The result is a vector perpendicular to both inputs.

Its magnitude is $\|u\|\|v\|\sin\theta$, the parallelogram area for edge vectors u and v. Reverse the order to negate the vector. A triangle uses half the area. Parallel vectors, including opposite directions, have zero cross product.

sections.heading: Handedness fixes the sign
paragraphs: The standard right-handed basis cycles i×j=k, j×k=i, and k×i=j. Reversing any of those ordered pairs changes the sign. A right-hand construction curls from the first nonparallel vector toward the second through the angle between them; the thumb gives the normal direction.

You can verify the sign algebraically without performing a hand gesture. In the xy plane, positive z corresponds to the orientation from +x toward +y. Two vectors with zero z components have cross vector (0,0,ux vy-uy vx). Keep this signed normal separate from the nonnegative area.

sections.heading: Compute all three components carefully
paragraphs: Each component subtracts a pair of products in a cyclic order. The middle component is uz vx-ux vz. If you expand a determinant by its first row, that same component comes from a negative cofactor; forgetting it is a common sign error.

A useful check is that the result dotted with u and with v is zero. This detects many arithmetic mistakes, although the zero vector also passes those checks. When the inputs are not parallel, an accidentally zero answer still needs inspection. Check the magnitude or compute one component independently.

sections.heading: Order changes orientation, not area
paragraphs: The equation v×u=-(u×v) is called anticommutativity. Unlike the dot product, the cross product cannot be freely reordered. Scaling an input scales the cross product, and a negative scale can reverse its direction.

The area of the parallelogram is the cross-product magnitude, so it is unaffected by reversing the edge order. The triangle determined by the same two edges has half that area. When the edges are parallel, the shape is degenerate and its area is zero; no unique normal direction is defined by the zero result.

sections.heading: Use the supplied torque model with a stated origin
paragraphs: For a force applied at position r measured from a specified origin, the supplied model is $\tau=r\times F$. Position goes first, force second. The vector records a rotational tendency about that origin; this refresher does not derive full rigid-body dynamics.

Torque has units N m and is a vector. Work from the previous lesson also has dimensions of force times length, but it is a scalar dot product and is conventionally reported in joules. Matching dimensions alone does not make these quantities interchangeable. Moving the reference origin generally changes r and can change the torque.

sections.heading: Use a picture and an algebraic check together
paragraphs: For a planar example, draw the two ordered edges, compute the signed z component, and state whether the normal points in +z or -z. Then take its absolute value for parallelogram area. The activity lets you swap order and observe both changes separately.

For spatial vectors, the component formula remains reliable when a flat sketch is hard to interpret. Keep the frame right-handed, show the operation order, carry units, and check perpendicularity. Use the full physics course for assumptions about forces and motion beyond the supplied model.
